metadata.title: Downfall: Fire, Texture and Shader Evidence

beats.narration_text: Hello. Liam, in for Bear. This is Downfall's shader assignment: a burning bottle driven by game state, a rusty cargo panel lit by the scene, and experiments that check what their pixels actually mean. The useful question is whether the rendered result follows the prediction.

show.event: Composer opens on the A5 demonstration prompt

props.command: Please use Walker to convert my game design document about Downfall's burning bottles and cargo panels into a shader demonstration with predictions, real engine results and failure checks.

beats.narration_text: A shader changes appearance. The game owns the state. The pixels follow rules. Measure the result. Three small programs make those rules visible in Downfall, and controlled comparisons check that they hold.

beats.narration_text: Spatial makes this a three-dimensional surface program. Unshaded keeps fire independent of lights. The project uses Forward Plus with Direct Three D twelve. Forward Plus supports the ground Decal and scene S S I L; Compatibility would lose both. Without an explicit assignment, ALBEDO is white. COLOR carries vertex color, not a sampled texture.

beats.narration_text: Here is the resulting flame over the city. This is an appearance layer over the existing hazard. The background remains visible through the additive shape. Writing an explicit fire color gives this yellow center; simply forwarding a plain quad's white vertex color would not produce the same result. This controlled view uses Linear tone mapping.

show.event: The real city and the controlled r=1 flame

beats.narration_text: This is the required color statement, unchanged. Remaining fire mixes red embers toward yellow heat and multiplies by intensity. Alpha is a separate decision: the shape and remaining fraction determine coverage. Fragment evaluates that shape across the surface. Moving its nonlinear shape calculation to four corner vertices would change the interpolated outline.

show.event: Read source lines 17-18, then follow their consequence in the next beat

props.title: Color And Coverage
props.code:
ALBEDO = mix(ember_color.rgb, hot_color.rgb, fire_remaining) * intensity;
	ALPHA = clamp(shape * clamp(fire_remaining, 0.0, 1.0) * flicker, 0.0, 1.0);

beats.narration_text: Now compare the three controlled values. At the center, full fire measures two ten, two ten, sixty seven. Half fire is one fifty eight, one twenty one, sixty seven. Zero returns the original background. Those are the values predicted before capture. Setting two produces a green channel of two fifty five: the Inspector range did not clamp the program's input.

show.event: r=1, 0.5, 0 and 2 appear in order with their measured center samples

beats.narration_text: The CPU connection is four lines. After the hazard updates, this driver checks whether simulation is active, divides remaining duration by the cached initial duration, clamps the ratio, and writes the material parameter. It has no second damage timer. Every fire owns a material, while all of those materials share the same Shader resource.

show.event: Read source lines 40-43, then follow their consequence in the next beat

props.title: State Enters Through A Uniform
props.code:
func _physics_process(_delta: float) -> void:
	if not is_instance_valid(hazard) or not is_instance_valid(hazard.game): return
	if not hazard.game.simulation_active(): return
	_material.set_shader_parameter("fire_remaining", clampf(hazard.lasting / initial_lasting, 0.0, 1.0))

beats.narration_text: Watch the bottle land, then the flame appear above its ground mark. The thrower keeps making new fires instead of restarting one shared color. During the pause, the lifetime value holds while the visual flicker can continue. Nine fires were recorded in this run. The explosive slug keeps a warning and burst; it does not acquire a flame mesh.

beats.narration_text: A texture hint can change the numbers. These two samplers read exactly the same three pixels. The first declares source color and the other reads raw data. Both use nearest filtering and disable repetition, so texture filtering cannot explain the difference. The Boolean switches between the two paths without adding a correction factor.

show.event: Read source lines 4-9, then follow their consequence in the next beat

props.title: One Texture, Two Interpretations

beats.narration_text: The top row returns sixty four, one twenty eight, and one ninety two. The lower row is visibly brighter: one thirty seven, one eighty eight, and two twenty five. The original prediction matches every center sample exactly. Missing the first decode leaves the raw values to be encoded again for display. This is why an albedo hint belongs on the sampler.

show.event: The six real hint-experiment samples and the upper/lower gray panels

beats.narration_text: Cargo needs three different kinds of texture. Albedo is color. Roughness is scalar data. The normal map is encoded direction data. Only albedo gets source color. All three repeat and use the same filtering. The normal sample goes through Godot's normal-map path, rather than being decoded as a color or assigned directly to NORMAL.

show.event: Read source lines 3-5, then follow their consequence in the next beat

props.title: Color And Data Stay Separate

beats.narration_text: The normal comparison uses the same light and the same panel position. Raw Direct X reverses the green direction. Flipping its Y import setting makes it agree with the Open G L version within two display levels. The source map is very flat, so the visual difference is subtle. Raking light reveals it more clearly than the review light.

show.event: GL, raw DX and Y-corrected DX under review and raking light

beats.narration_text: Here the surface stays lit. One scaled UV feeds all three textures, so a rust patch and its normal detail keep the same size. Roughness is clamped after scaling because the control reaches two. Normal strength goes to NORMAL MAP DEPTH. The shader writes no alpha and no metallic value, keeping the panel opaque and nonmetallic.

show.event: Read source lines 16-21, then follow their consequence in the next beat

props.title: Four Controls, One UV

beats.narration_text: The scan makes the trade-offs visible. Small UV scale magnifies a small part of the sheet; eight repeats make the rust look much finer. Black tint hides most diffuse detail. Roughness two clips much of this map to fully rough. Normal strength two changes the raking light slightly, but cannot invent large dents that are absent from the texture.

show.event: Minimum, default and maximum settings across the four cargo controls

beats.narration_text: These values live on a material instance. The Shader holds declarations and defaults; a ShaderMaterial holds the current overrides and texture bindings. Two boxes can therefore use one program with different responses. Sharing the material itself would share the override too. The experiment changes the common program first, then changes only the first material's tint.

show.event: Read source lines 10-17, then follow their consequence in the next beat

props.title: The Material Holds The Overrides
props.code:
shader = ExtResource("1_1coxp")
shader_parameter/albedo_tex = ExtResource("2_xq0y5")
shader_parameter/roughness_tex = ExtResource("4_hs00n")
shader_parameter/normal_tex = ExtResource("3_wus1a")
shader_parameter/uv_scale = 1.0
shader_parameter/tint_color = Color(1, 1, 1, 1)
shader_parameter/roughness_scale = 0.65
shader_parameter/normal_strength = 0.35

beats.narration_text: First both panels respond when the shared shader's color statement changes. After restoring it, changing only A's tint alters the left panel; the right panel stays identical. This separates program sharing from value sharing. The actual base uses those two independent materials on crate stacks. Under its A C E S lighting, the weathered stack is darker.

show.event: Baseline → common shader edit → restored → A-only parameter edit → actual base

beats.narration_text: Godot's generated version reaches the same surface outputs with more general controls. It chooses a roughness channel, scales the sample, then assigns the normal texture and its depth. Its color sampler also declares source color, and its normal sampler does not. Saving the Shader alone does not save the converted material's texture bindings and current values.

show.event: Read source lines 41-47, then follow their consequence in the next beat

props.title: Compare The Generated Program

beats.narration_text: This BoxMesh is rendered with that generated program and the three bound textures. It parses and draws, but it is kept out of the game. The hand-written cargo program has fewer controls because it solves a narrower job. The comparison also shows why a generated declaration is not a complete material: the textures and parameter overrides still have to be supplied.

show.event: The generated shader's actual BoxMesh rendering

beats.narration_text: Frame counting would be a different timer. One hundred eighty rendered frames last six seconds at thirty frames per second, three at sixty, and one point two five at one forty four. This driver reads the existing physics state instead. Its measured endpoint is one hundred eighty one physics steps, the same at all three render rates.

show.event: Rows appear as each frame-rate lifetime is explained

props.title: 180 Rendered Frames
props.note: Actual hazard: 181 physics steps / 3.016667 game seconds

beats.narration_text: Time has its own check. Over one hundred twenty frames at fixed sixty, shader TIME advances two seconds at normal speed, one at half speed, four at double speed, and zero with time scale zero. A normal game menu pauses this hazard through simulation active; it does not set engine time scale to zero. That is why flicker can continue while lifetime color holds.

show.event: The four measured time increments appear in narration order

props.title: Shader TIME Follows Time Scale
props.note: 120 frames at fixed 60 fps; values decoded from rendered pixels

beats.narration_text: The useful result is a small, testable connection from state to appearance. The fire predictions match. The texture hints change the expected pixels. Separate materials keep separate values. Limits remain visible: the normal texture is subtle, the system capture needed a different Windows path, and the old regression failures remain in the report. Those limits belong beside the successful checks.
